chapter: Cab Calloway on the road and segregation
title: Segregation on tour: living on the Pullman, and not bitter
summary: The band could not stay in hotels or eat in white restaurants, so they kept a Pullman and found colored restaurants. As a Southerner he expected it, recalls being threatened in Nashville and Claude Jones passing in a restaurant, and says it bothered Northern musicians more.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Uh-huh. What about the hotels, that must've been a problem...
Well, we couldn't stay at hotels, we just had to -- that's why we had the Pullman. We had a Pullman we kept all the time.
Cause you slept on the train?
Course, you slept on the train. So we weren't allowed to go anyplace to eat or anything, just had to find colored restaurants or eat -- have stuff brought to the car.
Didn't that make you bitter?
It didn't make me bitter, because I

was a Southerner, I was used to that. I'd been run out of places in Nashville, as a kid. After playing a beautiful job, like out to the Belle Meade Country Club, I was coming out one night after finishing a job and we were (unintelligible) bringing the instruments, and a white girl and her boyfriend, people coming home from -- she said mister, can I beat on your drum and I said, Lady, no, she said -- and the guy said, well if we can't beat on that drum, we're going to beat on your head, so I put the drums, and I said, well you help yourselves (to beat on the drums). You know. I'm used to that because the Southerners never bothered me. I just know, how they are. So, travelling through the South never bothered me. I didn't expect to go walk into a restaurant, sit down and eat.

One day Claude Jones did it, though. Claude Jones, he could actually pass. Claude Jones did it -- we were side-tracked into this -- right across, old beat grease joint, Claude Jones, went on in the restaurant, sat down at the counter and they served him. We didn't do it, but he could pass.

So, I think Lamar Wright (unintelligible) spied him, you know, in there and I think Lamar Wright (unintelligible) somebody went in there and sat down by him and said oh, if Claude could go in there, so -- I think it was Lamar, went in there sat down beside him and the man, said what the hell are you -- you know and then ran Claude and Lamar out of the joint.
Hm.
Because you know you run into those
things.
Right.
But it never bothered me and I expected it, you know. But it made -- it upset some guys, but it didn't bother me. I knew what to do and I knew what was expected and it didn't bother me.
Hm.

See, I'd get my food and I'd go somewhere and buy something or go in the back of the restaurant and the man give it to me and I'd walk on out the door take it on back and eat it, in the bus. But it didn't bother me. But it would bother, I guess musicians that born in the North, you know, places like that.
Right.
It didn't bother me at all, not one bit.
Because you grew up with this?
Yeah, I grew up with it and that mess down there.
